title: How Generations See Privacy Differently
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Frames a major source of generational workplace friction as a philosophical disagreement about privacy: older generations treat it as a default right selectively given up, while younger generations, shaped by the internet, treat it as something actively constructed against a default of exposure. Works through concrete examples -- productivity monitoring, salary transparency, discussing mental health openly -- showing both generational reactions are rational given the different worlds each grew up in. The prescribed fix is for leaders to name explicit norms issue by issue (what's confidential, what's discretionary, what the organization will and won't disclose) rather than letting informal norms default to whoever holds power.
points: Generational conflict over privacy is a genuine philosophical difference -- privacy as a default right to selectively surrender versus privacy as something actively constructed against a default of exposure -- not simply one side being wrong.
Left unaddressed, informal privacy norms tend to default to the values of whoever holds power in the organization, favoring one generation over another.
The fix is issue-by-issue explicit norm-setting (compensation, performance metrics, personal crises) rather than a single blanket policy or unstated compromise.
quotes: Older generations tend to see privacy as a default right, something you start with and choose selectively to give up. Younger generations, shaped by the internet and social media, experience privacy as something you actively construct and manage in a world where the default is exposure.
An older team member who bristles at productivity monitoring isn’t simply resisting change. They believe their results should speak for themselves.

A younger team member who openly shares their salary or mental health struggles isn’t being reckless. They are operating from a framework in which transparency is a form of self-protection and community-building.
Most organizations fail to articulate what is and isn’t appropriate to share. So, norms emerge informally, usually reflecting the values of whoever holds power in the organization.

Unlike a general compromise, this is best done on an issue-by-issue basis. The norms should reflect what will likely work best for everyone on that particular issue, such as compensation, performance metrics, or a team member in crisis.
The best leaders bridge the privacy divide not by picking a side but by making the choice itself feel clear and safe.
